1:
Several commentators open with the psalm’s liturgical place, not its words. Keil and Delitzsch note that the Hallel begins here, recited at the three great feasts, at the Dedication and at the new moons, but not on New Year’s day or the day of Atonement, because a cheerful song of praise does not harmonise with those mournful solemnities; and only in fragments during the last days of the Passover, since God’s creatures were drowned in the sea and it is no time for songs of rejoicing. In the Passover night it is divided in two, one half sung before the repast and the other after the fourth cup—to which the hymn sung after the institution of the Lord’s Supper may refer. Adam Clarke gives the same grouping with a different boundary, counting six psalms as the great Hallel and identifying it with the hymn the evangelists say Jesus and his disciples sang; he thinks it composed after the return from the captivity, and notes that it has no title but Hallelujah. John Calvin reports the tradition on the authority of a bishop who supposed the Great Hallel to include this and the five following psalms, and passes on a note about authorship: since two verses are taken from the song of Hannah and a third alludes to her history, it might be by Samuel or David, so nearly interested in the mercies vouchsafed to her. John Gill observes only that the opening word is the psalm’s title, as in the two preceding.

The servants summoned are variously identified. Charles Ellicott takes them for Israel; Clarke thinks the address probably to the Levites, and adds that an old English version renders the line praise the Lord, ye knaves, the word having then meant a servant. Matthew Henry answers that if it be the Levites, all Christians are a royal priesthood to show forth the praises of him who called them; he includes the angels, though they need no calling from us. Those who attend him as servants know him best and receive most of his favours, and it is easy pleasant work to speak well of their Master. C.H. Spurgeon presses it harder: prayer is the myrrh and praise the frankincense, and both must be presented—how can we pray for mercy hereafter if we do not bless God for his love in the past? Those who were slaves of Pharaoh groaned by reason of their bondage, but as servants of the Lord they were to express themselves in songs of joy; and they praise God best who serve him best, since service is praise. Augustine of Hippo takes the children of the opening line and will not let older hearers exempt themselves: they are not to think the exhortation misses them because they are in the prime of manhood or growing grey, for the Apostle bids all be children in malice and men in understanding—the malice being pride, which will not walk the narrow path, while a child enters easily.

The two boundaries, time and place, are read plainly and largely. Augustine imagines a child asking why the blessing runs from this time forth and not from before all ages, and answers that it begins the moment the words are spoken. Henry draws the lesson forward: let not the work die with us, but let us be doing it in a better world and those after us doing it here. On the second boundary Gill insists the words mean place and not time, all the space between the rising and the setting sun, so that all within that compass are creatures of God and bound to praise him—though many have worshipped the sun itself. Clarke allows both readings. Henry hears in the two verses a glimpse of the kingdom of glory and then of the kingdom of grace, when the church shall no longer be confined to the Jewish nation.
4:
The exaltation is stated in two directions, over the nations and over the heavens, and the commentators take the pairing as deliberate. Keil and Delitzsch read it as a confirmation of the praiseworthiness just asserted: the totality of the nations is great, but Jahve is raised above it; the heavens are glorious, but his glory is exalted above them. They resist assimilating the line to a parallel elsewhere, holding instead that the word for exalted governs the second half as well as the first, so that he is the incomparable One who has set his throne in the height and at the same time directs his gaze deep downwards—nothing in all the realm of the creatures beneath him escaping his sight, and nothing being so low that it remains unnoticed. John Gill gives the first half its political sense: he is the most High in all the earth, higher than the highest, King of kings and Lord of lords, all nations being made by him and under his dominion, and in comparison of him as the drop of a bucket and the small dust of the balance; and he takes the verse to look forward to the time when the Lord shall be more visibly King over all the earth. Adam Clarke compresses the same point into an inference—he governs all and provides for all, therefore let all give him praise—and Charles Ellicott simply refers the reader to an earlier psalm on the same theme.

The question that follows is treated as the hinge of the psalm. Gill answers it by ranging over the possible rivals—the gods of the nations, the angels of heaven, the mighty monarchs of earth—and finds none like him for the perfections of his nature or for the works of his hands in creation, providence and grace; what makes the reflection the more delightful to good men, he adds, is that this God is their God. Clarke turns the same question into an argument from ordinary experience: those who are highly exalted are generally unapproachable, proud and overbearing, or so surrounded with magnificence and flatterers that the poor have no access to them; but God, though infinitely exalted, humbles himself to behold even heaven, and much more when he condescends to behold earth and its inhabitants, so loving his creatures that he rejoices over even the meanest of them to do them good. Ellicott makes the contrast explicitly religious rather than social, setting this condescension against the indifference to human joys and sorrows which the heathen deities were said to show. John Wesley states it as sheer disproportion: he is so high that it is a wonderful condescension in him to take any notice of his heavenly host, and much more of sinful and miserable men upon earth.

Gill alone works the downward look out in detail, and he does it by descending through the heavens by stages. The highest heavens hold the angels, whom God upholds in their beings and admits into his presence, delighting in their persons and accepting their services—which, though pure, are still creature services, and it is condescension to accept them, since the angels themselves are as nothing in comparison of him and veil their faces before him; glorified saints, he adds, are continually in his view and favoured with intimate communion. Then he humbles himself to look lower, to the starry heavens, preserving the sun and moon and stars in their being, directing their courses, continuing their influence, bringing out their host by number and calling them by their names, so that because of his power not one fails. Lower still he beholds the things in the airy heavens, where there is not a meteor or cloud that flies, or a wind that blows, but he observes, guides and directs it.
7:
The turn to the poor is traced by everyone to the song of Hannah. Keil and Delitzsch say the thoughts of these verses are transplanted from it, and identify the images: dust is an emblem of lowly estate, the word rendered dunghill an emblem of the deepest poverty and desertion. They explain it from a custom still observable, that the man shut out from society lies upon the mezbele, the heap of dung or ashes, by day calling on passers-by for alms and by night hiding in the ashes the sun has warmed. The poet has Hannah’s own exaltation out of sorrow and reproach before his eye, they add, though he does not repeat the words of her song that refer to it. Charles Ellicott quotes the same description at length, rendering the word literally as a heap of rubbish: before each village in Hauran the household heaps up the sweepings of their stalls until it rises far above the highest buildings; the mezbela serves as a watch-tower, and on close oppressive evenings as a place of assembly because there is a current of air on the height; there the children play all day, and there the forsaken one lies who, seized with some horrible malady, may not enter the dwellings of men. It was on the mezbela, he notes, that tradition says Job sat.

The raising itself is read historically and spiritually. Adam Clarke takes it plainly, that the poorest man in the most abject circumstances is an object of God’s merciful regards, and thinks the words may allude to the captives in Babylon, whom God raised out of that dust and dunghill; others, he notes, apply it to the resurrection of the dead. John Gill divides it in two. Persons of mean extraction are sometimes raised to great honour, as Saul and David were; and the words are true also of those spiritually poor and needy, as all men are, though not all are sensible of it—these being called poor in spirit, pronounced blessed, and raised out of the dust of sin and self-abhorrence in which they lie when convicted of it. On the seating with princes he keeps to the spiritual sense: all the saints are princes by birth, sons of the King of kings, born of God and not of the will of man, having the spirit of adoption and not of bondage, and heirs of a kingdom; those raised from a low condition are set among such princes here, brought to Zion and given a name in the house of God better than that of sons and daughters, and set among princes hereafter. Clarke reads the word for princes with an antiquarian eye, noting that an old English version renders it the aldermen, the most respectable of the people. John Wesley keeps the historical instances—as he did Joseph and David—and adds that God’s people are in his account far more honourable than the princes of heathen nations.

The last verse closes with a domestic image, and the readings run from the literal to the national. Gill notes that several versions render the phrase to dwell in the house, but prefers the sense of causing the house to be inhabited, building it up as the barren woman does when made fruitful, as Rachel and Leah built up the house of Israel; and he applies it to the church of God. Clarke takes it as a figure for the desolate state of the captives in Babylon and the happy change on their return, remarking that these are nearly the words of Hannah. Ellicott supplies the social fact that makes the promise weighty—motherhood alone assured the wife a fixed and dignified position in her husband’s house—and says the quotation from Hannah’s song suggested the allusion to her story; we are right, he concludes, in taking this joyful mother as emblematic of the nation restored to prosperity and joy.
